The node is for street level water and the team is led by Chen Pan. It harvests its own solar power and carries temperature, humidity, light and precipitation sensing plus four optical water level sensors at different heights. It runs a compressed machine learning model on the microcontroller itself rather than sending readings to a server. It reports over long range radio instead of a cell tower, so it keeps warning when the grid and the network are down, which is when the water rises. The work was funded in part by a Texas Coastal Management Program grant from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. It is a prototype and the announcement names no place that has installed one.

items.title: ERCOT starts sending the Batch Zero questionnaires, and a data center that does not answer comes off the list
items.content_text: ERCOT issued a market notice on September 9th, 2026. It states that the grid operator has begun sending Batch Zero Verification Requests for Information. They go to a majority of the large load entities whose loads were conditionally included in Batch Zero. The notice states that completing the verification is a condition of staying in Batch Zero. Batch Zero is the group of large loads whose place in the interconnection study was frozen pending the audit the Governor directed in August.

items.title: Federal energy department opens comment on securing the grid and names AI as why demand grew, closing October 9th
items.content_text: The Department of Energy published a request for information on September 9th, 2026. It implements an August 26th executive order on securing the United States bulk power system. The notice asks about covered equipment and transactions and about foreign produced bulk power system electric equipment. It also asks about remote access practices and federal procurement. The notice names advanced manufacturing and data centers and artificial intelligence and defense production as what increased the nation's dependence on reliable electricity. Written responses are accepted through October 9th, 2026 and a public webinar is set for September 16th.

items.title: Federal survey office asks whether the household internet survey should start measuring AI use, closing November 9th
items.content_text: The National Telecommunications and Information Administration submitted its Internet Use Survey to the Office of Management and Budget for renewal on September 9th, 2026. It asked the public directly whether more data is needed on artificial intelligence. The notice names AI use at work or home and attitudes toward AI as areas it is asking about. Comments must be received on or before November 9th, 2026.

items.title: Texas Children's and UT Southwestern radiologists publish that imaging AI has largely skipped children
items.content_text: An expert panel review in the American Journal of Roentgenology states that pediatric medical imaging remains substantially underrepresented across artificial intelligence in radiology. The panel means the development of models and their validation and their regulation and their use in the clinic. Two of its authors are Texas radiologists. One works in the radiology department shared by Baylor College of Medicine and Texas Children's Hospital in Houston. The other is at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas. The panel gives its reason plainly. Children go through continuous physiologic and anatomic changes that adults do not, so a model trained on adults is not the model a child needs. It names what holds pediatric work back. Public datasets are scarce and institutional data is fragmented and external validation is insufficient. It also names off-label use of adult-trained AI models among the ethical and regulatory concerns in children. The review is a recommendation document rather than a hospital policy. No Texas institution has published a purchasing change that follows from it.

items.title: An MD Anderson and UT Medical Branch MRI model scored lower on patients it was not built on
items.content_text: The authors include radiologists at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston and at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston. They built a machine learning survival model from MRI radiomic features and tested it on a separate patient group without refitting it. Its discrimination score was lower on the group it was tested on than on the group it was built on. The paper reports overlapping confidence intervals for the two and no test that the difference is real. The authors conclude that the approach showed limited standalone discrimination and support cautious use of it as an exploratory imaging biomarker. The paper is a research result rather than a deployment, and neither institution has published a statement that the model is used in patient care.

items.title: Memorial Hermann clinicians send Houston patients an AI drafted explanation of their own test results
items.content_text: Memorial Hermann Health System says its clinicians are using an artificial intelligence assistant built into Epic to draft the note a patient receives with a lab or imaging result. The draft is written in plain language rather than clinical terms and the clinician can review, edit and personalize it before sharing it with the patient. The health system reports that patients sent 32% fewer follow up messages about test results when the clinician started from the draft. It reports the tool has helped care teams write over 55,000 messages and that clinicians starting from a draft saved an average of nine seconds per result comment. The feature was piloted in December of 2025 in the system's innovation clinic and use has since expanded across the system. A health system trade publication that read the same announcement noted every one of those figures comes from the software vendor and its customer. No baseline, control arm or denominator is published beside them, and the share describes only the clinicians who chose to work from a draft. The system's chief medical information officer says the technology is designed to support rather than replace the clinician's judgment.

items.title: The National Science Foundation funds a UT Austin center to put assistive robots into occupied homes, workplaces and care facilities
items.content_text: The National Science Foundation has made a Science and Technology Center award to the University of Texas at Austin for the Center for Human and Robot Co-Adaptation. Joydeep Biswas is the principal investigator. The award record runs from September 1st, 2026 to August 31st, 2031. The center's stated purpose is to work out how robots and the people around them adapt to each other over long periods. The aim is that assistive and service robots stay safe and aligned with what people actually want. The award abstract commits the work to a network of always on living laboratories in residential, commercial and healthcare buildings rather than to laboratory testing alone. The abstract says those deployments will grow more complex over the life of the center. The abstract describes the facility network as a thing to be built and the award clock started this month.

items.title: Governor directs the water board to enforce the state water use survey against data centers that did not return it
items.content_text: The Office of the Governor issued a directive to the Texas Water Development Board on September 14th, 2026. It tells the board to enforce the water use survey requirement against major water users, naming data centers. The directive covers failures already made as well as future ones. The reason the directive gives for needing the numbers is the state water plan. The board writes it and can't do that while it is denied detail on what is consumed now and what will be. That sentence is the Governor's office describing the board's position rather than the board speaking. The Texas Water Code requires a complete and accurate water use survey. A recipient who does not complete and return it commits an offense punishable as a crime. One who returns it late becomes ineligible for TCEQ permits, amendments or renewals under Chapter 11 of that code. The board is told to refer noncompliance to the County or District Attorney and to notify TCEQ for possible permit disqualification. It is also told to partner with the grid operator on the data center audit the Governor ordered on August 3rd, 2026. It must report back on its enforcement by October 14th, 2026.

items.title: UT Arlington replaces its business analytics degrees with artificial intelligence degrees
items.content_text: The University of Texas at Arlington College of Business launched two artificial intelligence degrees on September 14th, 2026. They are a bachelor's program and a master's program in artificial intelligence. The new degrees take the place of the college's existing Business Analytics programs rather than sitting beside them. The college describes a redesigned curriculum aimed at using the technology for business strategy, productivity and decision making. New certificate offerings accompany the degrees. No start term and no first cohort size is stated in the announcement.

items.title: Grid operator asks the water board's questions and gives data centers until October 12th
items.content_text: ERCOT issued Market Notice M-B091426-01 on September 14th, 2026, opening a Request for Information on the state and community impacts of data centers. Its stated audience is developers of data centers of 25 MW and larger. The body narrows the actual recipients to two defined groups rather than every developer of that size. It is issued jointly with the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the Texas Water Development Board. Section C carries the water questions. The water board's Executive Administrator authorized the grid operator to ask them on the board's behalf, and the grid operator forwards the answers back. A developer does not file its own response. Its transmission or distribution provider files it, with a notarized attestation, through the operator's own web platform. Responses are due at 5 p.m. Central Prevailing Time on October 12th, 2026. Not responding is reported to the commission and to the Office of the Governor, and under Texas Water Code 16.012 an incomplete answer to Section C carries criminal exposure. The notice states in its own words that this is a separate request from the Batch Zero eligibility one issued on September 9th, 2026. A report on what the answers show is expected by December 10th, 2026.

items.title: El Paso orders every city-sited license plate reader taken down and bars its city manager from signing another one
items.content_text: The El Paso City Council passed two directions to the city manager on September 15th, 2026. The first orders the removal within 60 days of all Flock Safety fixed automated license plate reader cameras and related hardware. That covers city property, city right of way and anything otherwise within the city's control. It reaches that hardware whoever owns it. The second bars the city manager from entering, executing, renewing or extending any such contract, unless the council directs otherwise. That covers Flock Safety and any other provider of fixed networked automated license plate readers or substantially similar technology. It also orders the city attorney to draft and return a resolution to the council within 30 days to further effectuate that direction. Both items were sponsored by members of the city council rather than brought by staff, and the council's own agenda records both as amended and passed.

items.title: Richardson ISD drafts a legislative ask that puts classroom AI guidance first
items.content_text: The Richardson Independent School District board reviewed a draft of the district's 2027 legislative priorities at its September 18th, 2026 meeting. The draft is built on three areas and the first of them is the responsible use of technology and artificial intelligence. That priority asks the Legislature for resources and guidance for the thoughtful use of artificial intelligence in education, alongside age appropriate approaches to screen time. The district says it gathered the input behind the draft through community roundtables with parent teacher associations, local chambers of commerce, higher education partners and other community organizations. The board is expected to vote on the final priorities on October 15th. The draft asks for resources and guidance and does not say what the state already provides, so nothing here establishes whether any exists. That is what makes this a record of where classroom AI rules are actually being written.

items.title: The National Science Foundation puts Texas Southern University in charge of one of five regional nodes in a new HBCU network for AI and quantum science
items.content_text: The National Science Foundation made a cooperative agreement to Texas Southern University in Houston for the HBCU AI and Quantum Innovation Network. The award record carries an award date of September 17th, 2026 and a start date of October 1st, 2026. Clark Atlanta University leads the network. The work runs through five regional nodes and Texas Southern leads one of them. Daniel Vrinceanu is the principal investigator. The stated work is identifying institutional strengths and needs. It also covers regional meetings and workshops. It covers shared training resources and pathways for students and faculty into these fields. The award sits in the foundation's Directorate for Technology, Innovation, and Partnerships.

items.title: The National Science Foundation funds a Texas A&M project to build AI digital twins of small and mid-sized water systems
items.content_text: The National Science Foundation made a standard grant to the Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station in College Station. The work is AI enabled digital twins of freshwater infrastructure under cascading hazards. The award record carries an award date of September 9th, 2026 and a start date of September 15th, 2026. It expires on August 31st, 2029. Sudipta Chowdhury is the principal investigator. The abstract describes water infrastructure that is getting harder to run. It names aging assets and deferred maintenance. It names climate driven hazards and power outages and water quality variability. A disruption that starts in one component can propagate through the connected networks. The abstract says current utility practice leans on monitoring systems and historical records and reactive emergency protocols. Those give limited ability to anticipate how a local anomaly escalates. The award sits in the foundation's Division of Civil, Mechanical, and Manufacturing Innovation.

items.title: Governor directs the environmental agency to issue no data center permits until the grid audit is done
items.content_text: On September 21st, 2026 the Governor directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to suspend action on all permits sought by data center projects. In the Governor's own words the agency will issue no permits sought by data center projects until they complete the grid and water board audits. The letter goes wider than one agency. It states that no other state agency is to move forward with regulatory approvals related to data centers until that information is acquired. The agency must report to the Office of the Governor on its compliance by October 19th, 2026.

items.title: PUCT open meeting calendar published as a live feed through mid 2027
items.content_text: The Public Utility Commission publishes its open meetings and public comment deadlines as a machine readable feed. Every entry is marked open to the public and names the room. The schedule runs into 2027, so a reader can see in advance when the commission will take up large load and transmission matters. The listings move as the calendar firms up, and an entry comes off the feed once its date has passed. The September 11th, 2026 open meeting has gone that way since the record last read the feed. The next open meeting the public may attend is Friday, September 18th, 2026 in the commissioners hearing room. Project 59550 stands on the feed with a comment deadline of September 17th, 2026 and Project 59086 with one of October 15th, 2026. It also carries a workshop on September 22nd, 2026, and it carries the grid operator's own board meetings at a separate address. No feed entry names a docket number, so the agenda published for each meeting is where a reader finds out what will be taken up.

items.title: National Science Foundation funds Rice to let AI propose numerical algorithms only where a proof checker certifies them
items.content_text: The National Science Foundation made a standard grant to William Marsh Rice University in Houston on August 17th, 2026. The award record describes reinforcement learning and large language models proposing randomized numerical linear algebra algorithms. The Lean proof assistant is required to certify correctness and cost before a candidate counts. The record states that the machine methods can explore designs efficiently but may produce opaque or inconsistent results without dependable guarantees. It also describes separating real algorithmic improvement from variation caused by the model itself. The award runs from September 15th, 2026 to August 31st, 2029.

items.title: Senate Economic Development cancels its September 3rd hearing on AI and the Texas workforce and resets for September 22nd
items.content_text: The Senate Committee on Economic Development carries an interim charge on preparing the Texas workforce for artificial intelligence. The charge directs the committee to study what AI does to the Texas workforce and what that means for the state's economic competitiveness. It also directs the committee to look at workforce resiliency. Educational pathways set against evolving employer needs and opportunities for upskilling are named in the same charge. The hearing the committee had set for Thursday, September 3rd, 2026 is canceled. The Legislature's own upcoming meetings listing now carries the committee for Tuesday, September 22nd, 2026 in hearing room E1.016 at the Capitol and marks it a public hearing. Angela Paxton chairs the committee and Kevin Sparks is vice chair.

items.title: El Paso City Council approves two plate reader items as revised, with the amendment text unpublished
items.content_text: The El Paso City Council took up two items filed by members of the council at its September 15th, 2026 meeting. The council's own record marks each one approved as revised. The amendments were made from the floor and their text is not published. The minutes are marked final and are not posted yet. What the revisions changed is not on a record a reader can reach today. As filed, the first item directed the City Manager to remove every Flock Safety fixed automated license plate reader camera from city property and right of way within 60 days. The hardware went with it, whoever owned the equipment. As filed, the second barred the City Manager from entering, renewing or extending any contract for fixed networked plate reader cameras or similar technology without a further council vote. It gave the City Attorney 30 days to draft a resolution carrying that out. Whether those terms survived the amendments is unconfirmed. El Paso sits outside the ERCOT region.

items.title: Energy Department funds a synthetic underground test pit at a Navasota drilling site to prove out mining automation
items.content_text: The Energy Department's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation named four mining proving ground projects on September 9th, 2026. One goes to Southern Methodist University, whose project location the announcement gives as Navasota, Texas. The department describes it as the world's first synthetic pit of its kind. It sits inside an existing instrumented drilling and sensing facility. Mining tools, workflows and automation systems can be tested repeatably in the field rather than only in a laboratory. The announcement states no dollar figure for the Texas project and never uses the words artificial intelligence, so what is funded here is automation testing rather than a model.

items.title: Science foundation funds a Texas A&M engineering station to build AI digital twins of small water systems
items.content_text: The National Science Foundation obligated an award to the Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station on September 9th, 2026. It sits in the Division of Civil, Mechanical, and Manufacturing Innovation. The work is to build AI-enabled digital twins that predict and manage cascading failures in freshwater infrastructure. The award record carries Artificial Intelligence among its programs. The performing site is College Station and the grant runs to August 31st, 2029. The abstract names no Texas utility. Which water system's data this reaches is not stated.

items.title: ERCOT tells its board that AI training loads can fatigue grid generators and drafts a limit on how fast their power draw may swing
items.content_text: The Electric Reliability Council of Texas put a list of emerging Large Load risks in front of its own Board of Directors at the September 14th and 15th, 2026 meeting. The presentation names three risks and a mitigation for each, and the three sit at three different stages. Ride through requirements are already in force. The model quality rule cleared the board on September 15th and now waits on the Public Utility Commission of Texas. The third rule has not been written yet. The grid operator states that Large Loads tied to data center AI training processes can swing their power draw fast enough to perturb synchronous generator shafts. It says that swing can cause equipment fatigue or damage. Its draft rule would hold a Large Load's power variation to 10 MW per 5 seconds. The same page states that the dynamic models the grid operator uses to study these loads have proven inaccurate, and that Texas A&M University is building better ones. The presentation itself was for information only and the board was asked to take no action on it.

items.title: Houston academic physician group moves from two ambient AI pilots toward one unified documentation platform
items.content_text: UT Physicians is the clinical practice of McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston. Its chief medical information officer told a school wide meeting on September 9th, 2026 that the practice is working toward adopting one ambient listening platform as a unified system. Pilots ran on two competing products first. The stated purpose is to cut the administrative load of clinical documentation and return attention to the patient. The same meeting reported that McGovern is taking part in a University of Texas System project examining already completed student simulations to see whether AI can write the feedback. Real time feedback is named as the longer term goal. No completion date is given for either.

items.title: UT Arlington builds a federally funded AI tutor that withholds the answer and helps build Fort Worth police training on the same method
items.content_text: The University of Texas at Arlington published an account on September 10th, 2026 of an AI conversational tutor built on a National Science Foundation grant. The tutor is designed not to supply an answer. It asks the student questions and offers hints so the student reaches the answer, in the way a teacher does at a desk. The same account says the researchers are helping to develop Fort Worth Police Department training using real life scenarios, with prompts based on the principles of de escalation. The university describes the system judging whether an officer is listening and whether the officer follows what the other person wants to talk about. No evaluation result is published for either use.

items.title: A three campus Texas trial tests whether a phone microphone held to the abdomen can count fetal movement by machine
items.content_text: A feasibility trial registered on the federal clinical trials registry is recruiting pregnant patients at three Texas academic campuses. The lead sponsor is a professor of women's health at the University of Texas at Austin. Participants place a smartphone microphone on the abdominal wall and the recorded audio is assessed by a machine rather than by the patient's own sense of movement. The registered design is a prospective observational feasibility study of 60 patients drawn from both low risk and high risk pregnancies. What it measures is whether the application is usable rather than whether it prevents any loss. The registration reports an earlier pilot of 205 patients in which the machine assessment outperformed maternal perception against simultaneous ultrasound. The record gives a study start of August 6th, 2026 and was last updated on September 14th, 2026.

items.title: UT San Antonio builds a solar powered flood sensor that runs its model on the device instead of a server
items.content_text: The University of Texas at San Antonio published an account on September 8th, 2026 of a field ready prototype flood warning node. A team led by an assistant professor of electrical engineering combined four things. Solar energy harvesting, environmental sensing, long range radio and a machine learning model compressed to run on the microcontroller itself. The design point is that the node evaluates flood risk where it stands rather than sending readings to a server. It keeps working when power and network fail in a storm. The university reports a validation accuracy figure from assessment after training rather than a measurement against a real flood. Funding is named as a Texas Coastal Management Program grant awarded by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The account names no installation site and no agency operating it, so what exists is a prototype.

items.title: Dallas issues its first code citations from the AI cameras on its brush trucks
items.content_text: The City of Dallas put AI enabled cameras on its sanitation brush trucks to photograph parcels from the public right of way and flag code violations. A December 9th, 2025 briefing to the council's Finance Committee set out the terms and drew a line under what the system would not be. It named automated ticketing and public safety surveillance among the three things it is not, and it stated that a human stands in the loop for all actions. The cameras went fully operational over the summer of 2026. A memo the city manager sent the council on September 8th, 2026 is reported to say that 57 citations have been issued at 34 properties. The same memo is reported to say that 39 of those citations went to three southern Dallas council districts. It is also reported to say the cameras scanned 10,000 properties and produced 3,700 violations that drew notices. The city's position is that the letters it sends are courtesy notices rather than warnings. The letter itself is reported to carry the words violations identified and to ask the owner to correct them to avoid further enforcement action. The assistant director of Code Compliance was asked about the difference and said you could call that a warning. The city manager briefs a council committee on the program on October 19th.

items.title: Leander stops paying for its plate reader contract and says the police department is no longer using the cameras or the data
items.content_text: The Leander City Council directed the city to discontinue funding its contract with the automated license plate recognition vendor Flock at its September 3rd, 2026 meeting. The city posted a notice saying that as of September 4th, 2026 the police department is no longer using Flock cameras or Flock data. The city's own account gives the reason as community concerns and says the system had been started to enhance public safety. What the notice does not say is what happens to the images already collected or whether the hardware comes down.

items.title: A Houston oil producer buys into an AI vendor and commits its Ward County operations to the vendor's system
items.content_text: Battalion Oil Corporation announced on September 8th, 2026 an equity investment in Collide Industrial Technologies and a Strategic Partner designation. Under an executed subscription agreement the producer will deploy the vendor's operations system across its upstream operations. The company says the deployment begins by unifying more than 100 terabytes of well files, land records, contracts and production history into one queryable model. The company says the work environment is expected to reach its production engineers at approximately day 90. The company names its Monument Draw cube development program in Ward County as the first fit. Every figure and every result in the announcement is the company's own and none of it has been through a regulator. The release names no client and no measured figure behind its claim of proven results.

items.title: The grid operator sends every conditionally classified large load a questionnaire, with a notarized attestation and ten business days to answer
items.content_text: ERCOT published the user guide for the Verification RFI on September 11th, 2026, the questionnaire it issues as part of the Batch Zero eligibility verification. The guide states the questionnaire goes to every large load that was conditionally classified on the list distributed to transmission service providers on September 3rd. Each of the three parties on a project, the load entity, the distribution service provider and the transmission service provider, answers the sections assigned to its own role. Which sections a project sees depends on the conditional classification ERCOT gave it. Every participating party has to upload a notarized attestation before the response can be submitted. Responses are due within ten business days of issuance and a five day extension may be requested through the transmission service provider. A load entity that fails to supply what its provider needs may be taken off the Batch Zero process. Only the transmission service provider can submit the finished response, and once submitted it is locked.

items.title: A data center developer tells its shareholders what the Batch Zero list did to five of its Texas projects, and one came back in a different class than it was filed in
items.content_text: Galaxy Digital published an account on September 8th, 2026 of the conditional Batch Zero classifications ERCOT gave five of its Texas data center projects. Three of the five sit at the Helios campus in Dickens County, in the panhandle region of West Texas. Two projects already approved at that campus before the batch were classified as Batch Zero Base Load. Three more, Caspian, Selene and a further Helios load request, were classified as Batch Zero Studied Load. The account states that the company submitted Caspian as Base Load and that it was conditionally classified as Studied Load instead. It states what separates the two classes. A base load project is modeled in the study and is not subject to further capacity allocation. A studied load project is subject to capacity allocation as part of the study. The grid operator's own notice of the classifications named no load and gave no total. This account is where the public first learned what a classification did to a named project. The company's own risk section states that a classification may be modified, withdrawn or not confirmed, and that a project may be removed from Batch Zero.

items.title: The University of North Texas takes a twenty million dollar gift and names a college of artificial intelligence after the donors
items.content_text: The University of North Texas announced a gift from Anuradha and Vikas Sinha and will name the Anuradha and Vikas Sinha College of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Analytics. The university describes the college as an academic hub focused on the development, application and responsible use of artificial intelligence, intelligent systems and data analytics. The gift creates six permanent endowments covering college leadership, student scholarships and other purposes the announcement lists. One of the donors holds a doctorate from the university. Nothing in the announcement names a faculty appointment made, a student enrolled in the named college or a research result. What is decided here is the money and the name rather than a program already running.

items.title: PUCT Docket 59315, Oncor application for a 765 kV transmission line across 22 counties
items.content_text: Oncor Electric Delivery has applied to amend its certificate of convenience and necessity to build the Dinosaur Switch to Longshore Switch transmission line. The application covers a corridor crossing 22 named counties in central and west Texas. The docket has drawn one of the largest volumes of landowner filings in recent PUCT practice. Those filings include intervention requests, protests and a county resolution. The commission has the docket set for discussion and possible action at its open meeting on August 21st, 2026. That meeting is in a hotel ballroom in Austin rather than in the hearing room. That meeting takes up two Oncor 765 kV applications and nothing else before it closes. The commission issued its order on August 28th, 2026, amending the certificate to include the line and approving route 559. The administrative law judges had found the utility did not fully comply with the public meeting rule for links added after that meeting. The commission read the rule to require only one meeting before the application was filed. The order records the transmission providers projecting an exponential increase in non oil and gas load in the Permian Basin region, named as cryptocurrency mining, data centers and hydrogen electrolysis.

items.title: Hays County Commissioners Court adopted a 180-day emergency water review period for high water use developments and created a review board
items.content_text: The Hays County Commissioners Court approved a resolution on June 23rd, 2026 establishing a 180-day emergency water protection review period for high water use development applications, including data centers. The same resolution creates a review board that evaluates those proposals and advises the court. Commissioners voted unanimously. The county has been operating under drought conditions and water use restrictions tied to declining aquifer levels, which is the stated reason for the measure. This is the counter-image to the incentive votes elsewhere in Central Texas, since a county here chose to slow its own review rather than speed it up.

items.title: Williamson County Commissioners Court granted Compal USA Technology a Chapter 312 abatement for a Georgetown server service center
items.content_text: The Williamson County Commissioners Court approved a Chapter 312 tax abatement incentive agreement for Compal USA Technology Inc. on April 15th, 2026. The county described the project as a server service center on approximately 33 acres at 1800 Aviation Drive in Georgetown. It is to support enterprise and cloud infrastructure needs, general warehousing and other work in the electronics, technology and medical device industries. Chapter 312 agreements are performance based, so the county does not grant the abatement until the company meets the required measures. The agreement sets a minimum capital investment of $35 million and requires no fewer than 100 full-time employees within three years. If the terms are met the county abates 30% of assessed value for 10 consecutive years, an estimated $526,010 over that period. The City of Georgetown approved its own incentives for Compal on December 9th, 2025.

items.title: El Paso City Council adopts a Data Center Policy Framework requiring a Special Permit for hyperscale projects
items.content_text: The El Paso City Council voted on July 20th, 2026 to adopt a Data Center Policy Framework. The resolution came through a City Council Work Session and passed on a motion by Representative Boyar Trejo. The framework routes future hyperscale data center applications through a Special Permit with public notice, City Plan Commission review and a public hearing. It sets standards on water use, energy demand, noise and lighting. It also eliminates local economic incentives for future hyperscale projects. Implementation has to return to council as ordinance amendments, so the framework by itself changes no rule until those pass. El Paso sits in the Western Interconnection served by El Paso Electric and is not on ERCOT.

items.title: Guadalupe County Commissioners Court unanimously approves ending the county's Flock Safety license plate reader contract
items.content_text: Guadalupe County Sheriff Joshua Ray asked the Commissioners Court for permission to terminate the county's contract with Flock Safety, and the court approved unanimously. Flock cameras read license plates automatically and alert deputies to vehicles of interest. Ray told the court his view of the technology has not changed and that the reason is cost. The county pays to replace cameras that keep getting vandalized while continuing to pay the monthly bill. Guadalupe County sits in the San Antonio metro area between Seguin and New Braunfels.

items.title: National Science Foundation names UT El Paso in the first round of CyberAICorps Scholarship for Service awards
items.content_text: The National Science Foundation announced the first awards under its CyberAICorps Scholarship for Service program on July 28th, 2026. The University of Texas at El Paso is on the list. UTEP's award is for a project on building an AI-integrated cybersecurity workforce. The scholarships cover tuition and pay an academic year stipend. Recipients owe one year of government service for each year of funding. Texas A&M University and The University of Texas at Dallas also received inaugural awards, which puts three of the first round institutions in Texas.

items.title: Wichita Falls Planning and Zoning Commission approves a conditional use permit for a DataNovaX data center on Airport Drive
items.content_text: The City of Wichita Falls Planning and Zoning Commission approved a conditional use request from DataNovaX. It lets the company put a data center inside an existing building at 2236 Airport Drive on the north side of the city. The building is a former grocery store and call center of about 37,000 square feet. City staff attached conditions rather than approving the use outright, and the largest was a ban on evaporative cooling, which forces an air cooled design and holds water use down. Development Services director Fabian Medellin said the applicant agreed to the limits, which also cover light pollution and electricity use. City officials put the load at 12 megawatts and the investment at an estimated 100 million dollars. The Airport Drive building is a first piece of a larger Pioneer Park project with a much bigger second phase planned.

items.title: Angelina County Commissioners Court adopts Resolution 010-26 asking the Legislature for authority over data centers
items.content_text: Angelina County Commissioners Court voted unanimously on July 14th, 2026 to adopt Resolution 010-26. It asks the Texas Legislature to grant counties specific powers over large scale industrial development that local government currently can't reach. The requests include buffer and setback rules, noise and heat attenuation standards, light pollution limits, water impact statements and public hearings. County Judge Keith Wright framed the problem plainly. Without an abatement the county has no control over a data center at all. He also said the ask was kept narrow on purpose because a broad one would fail. The resolution carries no force by itself and lands with a Legislature that is not in regular session.

items.title: Carson County Commissioners Court approves a phased tax abatement agreement with Fermi America for the Project Matador HyperGrid campus
items.content_text: Carson County Commissioners Court approved a tax abatement agreement with Fermi America for the Project Matador HyperGrid campus in the Texas Panhandle. The agreement is two sided and pays the county on both ends of the same facility. Fermi pays 3 dollars per square foot of data center improvements and from 2,500 to 2,750 dollars per megawatt of generating capacity. County Judge Dan Looten said the agreement covers 15 phases and could extend up to 25 years. Each completed phase enters its own 10 year abatement. Yearly training with local EMS and first responders is written into the deal. This corner of the Panhandle sits in the Southwest Power Pool rather than ERCOT, so the ERCOT interconnection and reliability rules a Texas reader would assume do not govern here.

items.title: Brazoria County Commissioners Court adopted a resolution stating conditions it wants on data center development
items.content_text: On June 9th, 2026 Brazoria County Commissioners Court adopted a measure on data center development. Its own agenda system records it as a resolution about data centers and related facilities in Texas. The item was introduced on May 29th, 2026, reached the court and was approved. Reporting on the resolution says the court supports responsible economic development, including appropriately designed and sited data centers. It also says no future data center should proceed without an independent impact assessment. A county resolution is not an ordinance and Texas counties have no zoning power outside city limits, so this sets a stated position rather than a rule. It came from the same court that had already refused the reinvestment zone behind the Old Ocean Datacenter and Bulldog Power abatement applications.

items.title: Houston-Galveston Area Council put AI consulting services on its HGACBuy purchasing catalog under contract AI05-26
items.content_text: HGACBuy is the cooperative purchasing program run by the Houston-Galveston Area Council. It publishes an active contract numbered AI05-26 titled AI Consulting Services. The term runs from May 1st, 2026 through April 30th, 2030. The catalog describes the work as comprehensive guidance through the array of possible solutions where artificial intelligence can be integrated. Five vendors are listed as awarded on the contract page. This is the procurement plumbing behind a lot of Texas government AI work. A contract vehicle is how a small city or district buys a service without running its own solicitation.

items.title: Texas Water Development Board denied a petition to give data centers their own water demand category and adopted the 2027 State Water Plan the same day
items.content_text: The Texas Water Development Board took up a petition for rulemaking on July 23rd, 2026. It asked the agency to project water demand for data centers and crypto mining as a standalone industrial category. The petition was filed by Margaret Hill and co petitioners, and the board denied it. At the same meeting the board considered adoption of the 2027 State Water Plan (Phase I), which contains no separate demand line for high density computing load. Board members noted that regional water plans feed the state plan and can be amended as better data arrives. The decision means the state's central water planning document carries data center demand folded inside broader categories rather than on its own.

items.title: San Angelo City Council caps data center cooling water by ordinance
items.content_text: San Angelo passed Ordinance 2026-078, which adds Section 11.02.043 to the city water service rules. It puts hard numbers on how much city water a data center may take for cooling. Initial cooling system fill can't exceed 8.0 gallons per square foot of gross building area for each building. Routine makeup water can't exceed six percent of the installed cooling loop volume per building per calendar year, and cooling water has to be metered separately from other use. Any exceedance needs City Manager approval and has to be reported in writing to the City Council within five business days. The ordinance was introduced with a public hearing on May 19th, 2026 and passed on June 16th, 2026, taking effect the same day.

items.title: San Angelo writes data centers into its zoning code and makes them a conditional use only
items.content_text: San Angelo created Section 430 of its zoning ordinance, the first full land use rulebook for data centers in West Texas. New data centers are allowed as a principal use only by Conditional Use, and only in Light Manufacturing and Heavy Manufacturing districts. Each one comes back to a public hearing. The code caps buildings at 75 feet. It bars ground mounted equipment near residentially zoned property and limits noise to 55 dBa at the property line day and night. It also requires a sound modeling study before final site plan approval and a post development sound study after occupancy. The definition it adopted excludes cryptocurrency mining. The ordinance was introduced on May 5th, 2026 and passed on May 19th, 2026.

items.title: San Angelo sets reporting rules for data center coolant discharged into the city sewer
items.content_text: San Angelo adopted Ordinance 2026-076, which adds a data center subsection to the city's prohibited discharges rule. Any intentional release of treated cooling fluid into the sanitary sewer is defined as a discharge event, and sampling with laboratory verification has to be completed before each one. Records of volumes, results and dates must be kept for at least three years and handed to the Director of Water Utilities on request. Planned discharges need 72 hours written notice. Emergency discharges have to be reported within 4 hours with a written incident report inside 7 days. The council introduced the ordinance on May 19th, 2026 and adopted it on June 2nd, 2026.

items.title: PUCT Docket 59029, Oncor application for a second 765 kV line across ten west Texas counties
items.content_text: Oncor Electric Delivery has applied to amend its certificate of convenience and necessity to build the Longshore Switch to Drill Hole Switch transmission line. The application covers ten named counties in west Texas. The commission has it set for discussion and possible action at the open meeting on August 21st, 2026. That agenda carries this application and the Dinosaur Switch to Longshore Switch application and nothing else. The two lines meet at Longshore Switch. The commission issued its order on August 28th, 2026, amending the certificate to include the line and approving route 476. The two applications had been consolidated on the question of need and were severed again so each could take its own final order.

items.title: Brazos County Commissioners Court assigns the RELLIS data center tax abatement to ThisWay Global after the original developer's bankruptcy
items.content_text: Brazos County posted a Tax Code Section 312.207 notice that its Commissioners Court would consider assigning the tax abatement agreement for the RELLIS Campus data and research center. The agreement was originally approved on April 29th, 2025 with RELLIS Campus Data and Research Center, LLC. The pending assignee named in the notice is ThisWay, Global, Inc. The county's own notice puts the estimated cost of improvements and tangible personal property at a minimum of approximately 700 million dollars. The land sits in a reinvestment zone on the RELLIS campus. That campus belongs to The Texas A and M University System, so the abatement agreement is what decides whether the county collects anything from the build.

items.title: Frontera's queues close permanently on October 1st, 2026
items.content_text: The Texas Advanced Computing Center's Frontera user guide carries a warning. The queues close permanently on October 1st, 2026 after seven years of running. Users will still reach Frontera's file systems to transfer data off. Frontera is funded by the National Science Foundation through award 1818253 and the guide calls it the largest cluster dedicated to open science in the United States. The successor is Horizon. It is funded through the Leadership Class Computing Facility award. Horizon's own guide carries a notice dated in July saying it is still limited only to internal users. That guide also says it is in progress. Horizon lists three ways in. They are the facility's own allocations and the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource Pilot and the state's allocation system.

items.title: Brownsville takes up a temporary moratorium on data centers after staff tells the commission its code has no rules for them
items.content_text: At its September 1st, 2026 meeting the Brownsville City Commission considered starting the process for a temporary moratorium. It would cover data centers alongside private gaming clubs, automotive quick lube facilities, event centers and self storage. City staff told the commission that Brownsville's Unified Development Code contains no regulations addressing data centers. The stated purpose is to give the city time to study electricity and energy use, water consumption, noise, land use compatibility, infrastructure and economic and fiscal impacts. The proposal also reactivates the city's Environmental and Conservation Task Force to study data center development and recommend to the commission. The city's own account says an initial moratorium could run up to 90 days and could be extended for another 90 days after further proceedings.

items.title: Austin bars its city manager from buying any park camera or drone that depends on artificial intelligence
items.content_text: Austin City Council adopted Resolution No. 20260812-017 on August 12th, 2026. It directs the City Manager to write a Parks Security Implementation Plan. It also directs the manager to acquire and deploy security equipment for city parks and recreation lands. The resolution lists the kinds of equipment contemplated. Security cameras are on that list. So are non-recording drones as first responders. So are lighting and access control and signage and radio. The resolution then forbids the City Manager from considering any camera or drone system that depends on artificial intelligence to conduct surveillance or analysis. Anything acquired has to comply with the surveillance technology ordinance the council adopted in April. Parks with a history of violent crime are prioritized for the first deployment. The City Manager owes a progress update to the Council Climate, Water, Environment, and Parks Committee no later than December 9th, 2026. The resolution sets the date by which the update is owed and does not set a date for a meeting. The April ordinance the resolution points at is City Code Chapter 2-19. It already lists artificial intelligence or machine learning tools among what is not permitted. The exception is whatever the city's own policy allows.

items.title: Lubbock heard a citizen petition for an 18 month data center moratorium
items.content_text: The Lubbock City Council held a public hearing on September 8th, 2026 on a citizen petition brought under the city charter. The petition asks for an 18 month moratorium on high water use and high energy use data centers inside the city. The same agenda carried a separate resolution stating the council's desire that large scale data centers not be developed inside the municipal limits. That resolution waits on the council adopting regulations to protect public resources and public health and safety. A resolution states a desire and an ordinance states a rule, and the two items sat next to each other on the same agenda. The agenda and one speaker at the hearing are what is on the record so far. Neither says what the council did with either item.

items.title: The board takes a required high school money course to final adoption, and the text it published names AI tools in three of its chapters
items.content_text: The State Board of Education took the new Applied Personal Financial Literacy standards to second reading and final adoption. Its item for that is dated September 4th, 2026, and it publishes one attachment. That text tells a student to research career pathways using artificial intelligence tools. It tells the same student to explain how algorithm driven recommendations influence spending. It then asks that student to appraise automated investment platforms by analyzing their algorithmic limitations. Districts implement the course beginning with the school year that opens in 2027. The board found that the rule takes effect 20 days after filing with the Texas Register.

items.title: The grid operator tells providers which large loads it has provisionally placed in Batch Zero, and every placement carries a condition
items.content_text: ERCOT issued a market notice telling each Interconnecting Distribution Service Provider and Transmission Service Provider how it had provisionally classified the large loads submitted for the Batch Zero interconnection process. The notice states that inclusion is conditional. The conditions it names include the interconnecting large load entity passing verification and curing deficiencies in dynamic model data. Another is the Public Utility Commission of Texas granting a good cause exception. It states that failure to satisfy an applicable condition may disqualify the load. It also names the route by which an entity that disagrees with a classification may dispute it. The notice names no individual load and gives no total, so the size of the provisional list is not public.

items.title: Hays County posts the sheriff's promise not to switch on AI report writing without coming back to the court
items.content_text: The Hays County Commissioners Court agenda for September 1st, 2026 carried an item acknowledging that the Hays County Sheriff's Office had committed not to activate or implement Axon Draft One. The agenda describes that product as a report writing feature inside a vendor platform. The commitment reaches any new AI based feature the same platform may later offer under the related contract. What makes the item unusual is the condition rather than the refusal. Operational use requires returning to this court for approval, so the decision stays with the elected body rather than with the office holding the contract. The vendor's own product page describes the feature as drafting a report narrative from body worn camera audio. That page says an officer has to review and approve one before it can be submitted. The county's own Court Minutes archive for 2026 carries nothing later than July 28th, so the disposition is not on the public record today.

items.title: The Hays County Clerk asks the commissioners court to buy AI that writes the county's official minutes
items.content_text: The Hays County Commissioners Court agenda for September 15th, 2026 carried an item to authorize the County Clerk's Office to obtain AI Minutes through a vendor. The first year's amount is stated on the agenda. The same item asks the court to waive the county purchasing policy that requires three quotes, so the request is to buy this product without comparing it against others. The vendor's own site describes the product as using AI to write official meeting minutes from a recording, a live session or a pasted transcript. What the agenda does not say is whether a person reviews or certifies the machine's draft before it becomes the county's official record. That is the question the item leaves open. The county's own Court Minutes archive for 2026 carries nothing later than July 28th, so the disposition is not on the public record today.

items.title: Hays County takes up a policy on how it governs AI in surveillance
items.content_text: The Hays County Commissioners Court agenda for September 8th, 2026 carried an item on how the county governs its own use of artificial intelligence in surveillance. The item names equipment and software alongside the collection and analysis of data. It contemplated adopting a policy statement that would set guidelines and limits on the AI enabled surveillance technologies the county uses. The reach is general rather than product specific. That makes it the standing rule beside the narrower promise the same court posted a week earlier. The item immediately after it on the same agenda concerns two contract amendments with a different vendor. One of those is for report writing services. Nothing on either page connects the two. The county's own Court Minutes archive for 2026 carries nothing later than July 28th. The disposition is not on the public record today.
